info.title: BADI SOC API
info.description: API for BADI SOC: one platform for running a security operations centre and training the team that staffs it.

post.description: Sign in. Returns a JWT on success.

get.description: The signed-in user.

post.description: Sign out: revokes the current token until its own expiry passes.
Escalate an alert. The originating analyst comes from the token.

get.description:
The raw log lines behind an alert.

"Show me the logs" is the second thing any analyst asks, and until now the
answer was nothing: the platform held 50,000 Windows events, said so on
the overview, and had no way to show a single one.

An event belongs to this alert when it was linked at ingest, or when it
names one of the alert's addresses. The second is a correlation, not a
fact, so the response says which of the two produced each row rather than
presenting them as the same thing.
Return resolved/closed incidents as knowledge base patterns.
Find similar resolved incidents using TF-IDF + Jaccard hybrid similarity.
Return MITRE ATT&CK matrix with coverage computed from live alerts.
Build the incident response report for one incident.

Six KPI counts, issued in parallel.

Sequentially these cost six database round-trips; gathered they cost
roughly one.
Return live attacks derived from Alert.source_ip + country lookup.
Return threat map statistics computed from DB.

post.description: Record a shift handoff. The author comes from the token.

get.description: Handoffs addressed to the caller that nobody has acknowledged yet.

post.description: Acknowledge a handoff, which is what closes the loop on it.

get.description:
Return the live ECC register (Manager and L3 only).

The score is computed from compliance_controls and advances on its own as
the SOC works: resolved incidents, escalations and completed playbook runs
each raise the controls they are mapped to.

Export the register as a printable page (Manager and L3 only).

Open the URL, print, and choose "Save as PDF" to produce the file that is
submitted to the authority. Pass lang=ar for the Arabic edition.

200.description: HTML report — open in browser and use 'Print → Save as PDF' for NCA submission

get.description: Return analyst leaderboard (computed from analyst_point_events).

post.description:
Start a run of a playbook, owned by the caller and optionally tied to
an incident.

A run is what makes the playbook auditable afterwards: who followed which
procedure, for which incident, and which steps they actually completed.
Mark one step done. Who did it and when is recorded on the run.
Close the run, award points, and advance the mapped ECC control.

get.description: The caller's own runs, in progress and finished.

Every run carried out for this incident, by anyone.

Not filtered to the caller: an incident is worked by a team across shifts,
and the question this answers is what procedure the response followed, not
what one analyst did.
List all scenarios (without phase details).
Get the full scenario with its phases — without the answer key.

post.description:
Submit an answer for a phase. Returns feedback and the drill points.

This is the only place the answer key leaves the server, and only for the
option the analyst actually chose, once.

Close a run: grade every phase server-side and award scoreboard points.

The client sends which option it picked in each phase, never whether it was
right — the answer key is here, so the grade is computed here. A phase the
analyst never answered (the timer ran out, they left the drill) counts as
wrong, which is why an incomplete run is graded rather than rejected.

The three scoreboard actions are scenario-level, not phase-level, so this
is where they belong: submit_answer sees one phase and cannot know whether
the run passed.

Chat with BADI AI.

The role comes from the token, and the mode is checked against the
account's allowed modes, so training and live cannot leak into each other.

The assistant is also given a small snapshot of this centre's real state.
Without it, asked to summarise the dangerous alerts, it answered from the
general shape of a SOC — which in a security product means inventing an
incident.

get.description: Who is in the war room right now.

Enrich an IP address.

Training mode answers from the built-in dataset. Live mode queries
VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB and OTX, cached for 24 hours. A private, loopback or
reserved address is never sent anywhere, in either mode, so the endpoint
cannot be used to probe the internal network.

What this address has done on this estate.

Every alert that names the address as source or destination, the incidents
those alerts belong to, and the ATT&CK techniques they were mapped to. All
of it read from the platform's own records, so nothing here is inferred.

Whether a sign-in is required. Public: the sign-in screen itself needs it.

Never returns a credential, a role, or anything about a specific account.
It carries the standard envelope like every other endpoint — a bare object
here reads as a failure to the client, which then assumes a wall is up.
Liveness probe: OK while the process is running.
Readiness probe: checks the database connection and the API keys.

Which external services this deployment can actually reach.

Configured-or-not only: probing each provider on every page load would
spend quota to tell the reader something that changes when the .env
changes. The one live figure is the Gemini key count, which the client
already knows because it retires a key the service has rejected.

Never returns a key, or any part of one.

post.description: Seed the database. DEBUG only; in production run `python -m data.seed`.
